Concept. Misses are classified by cause. Compulsory misses are the first reference to a block and depend only on the reference stream. Capacity misses are the blocks a cache of that size cannot hold however it is organised. Conflict misses are blocks evicted only because too many of them map to the same set. Associativity attacks the third class alone.

Step by step.

  1. Total capacity and block size are fixed, so the number of blocks the cache can hold is unchanged and capacity misses cannot change.
  2. Each block is still seen for the first time once, so compulsory misses cannot change either.
  3. With 4 ways, up to four blocks that share a set can be resident, so blocks that a direct-mapped cache would have evicted on a conflict now survive: conflict misses can fall.
  4. Comparing four tags in parallel is slower than comparing one, so hit time rises slightly — it does not fall.

Answer: Option (A) — conflict misses can fall, capacity misses are unchanged.

Common misconception. Option (B) is the standard error: associativity does not create space, it only re-allocates the freedom to place a block. Option (D) inverts the real cost — associativity buys miss rate at the price of hit time and comparator hardware.

Takeaway. Associativity trades hit time for conflict misses; it does not touch capacity or compulsory misses.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 32 KB four-way set-associative cache uses 64-byte blocks. The byte address 0x00002A40 is presented to it. Which set does the address map to?
questions.question_html:
Question 6MCQharddirect-associative-setassociative-mappingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A 32 KB four-way set-associative cache uses 64-byte blocks. The byte address 0x00002A40 is presented to it. Which set does the address map to?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The set is selected by the block number, not by the byte address. Convert the address to a block number by dropping the offset bits, then reduce modulo the number of sets.

Step by step.

  1. Block offset = log2 64 = 6 bits, so the block number is the address shifted right by 6.
  2. 0x00002A40 = 10 816 in decimal; 10 816 / 64 = 169, so the block number is 169.
  3. Number of sets = 32 768 / (64 × 4) = 128.
  4. Set = 169 mod 128 = 41.
  5. Equivalently: the index field is bits 6 to 12 of the address, and 10 816 = 0b10_1010_0100_0000 gives index bits 1010101 = 85? — no: bits 6..12 are 0b0101001 = 41, which agrees.

Answer: 41 — set 41.

Common misconception. 169 is the block number, which is the answer only if you forget to reduce modulo the set count. 64 is the byte address reduced modulo 128, which mixes the offset into the index. Associativity is what makes the set count 128 rather than 512; using 512 sets would leave the block number unchanged at 169.

Takeaway. set = (address / block size) mod (capacity / (block size × ways)).

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle, a miss rate of 4% and a miss penalty of 50 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
questions.question_html:
Question 7MCQeasycache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 1

A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle, a miss rate of 4% and a miss penalty of 50 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
options: 2.0 cycles
3.0 cycles
3.5 cycles
5.0 cycles
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Average memory access time is the hit time plus the expected extra cost of a miss: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.

Step by step.

  1. Miss rate = 0.04, miss penalty = 50 cycles.
  2. Average miss cost = 0.04 × 50 = 2 cycles.
  3. AMAT = 1 + 2 = 3 cycles.
  4. Read as a weighted average: 96% of accesses cost 1 cycle and 4% cost 1 + 50 = 51 cycles, giving 0.96 × 1 + 0.04 × 51 = 3.

Answer: 3.0 cycles.

Common misconception. 2.0 cycles is the average miss cost alone; the hit time must be added. 5.0 cycles comes from multiplying the hit time by the miss rate instead of using the hit rate, which double-counts the miss.

Takeaway. AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty; the weighted-average form gives the same number.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: An L1 cache has a hit time of 1 cycle and a local miss rate of 5%. Its misses go to an L2 cache with a hit time of 10 cycles and a local miss rate of 20%; L2 misses go to main memory, which costs 100 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
questions.question_html:
Question 8MCQmediumcache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 1

An L1 cache has a hit time of 1 cycle and a local miss rate of 5%. Its misses go to an L2 cache with a hit time of 10 cycles and a local miss rate of 20%; L2 misses go to main memory, which costs 100 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
options: 1.5 cycles
2.0 cycles
2.3 cycles
2.5 cycles
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. With a two-level hierarchy the L1 miss penalty is itself an average access time for the lower level. Local miss rates multiply down the hierarchy; the cost of an L1 miss is L2 hit time + (L2 local miss rate × memory cost).

Step by step.

  1. Cost of an L1 miss = L2 hit time + L2 local miss rate × memory cost = 10 + 0.20 × 100 = 10 + 20 = 30 cycles.
  2. AMAT = L1 hit time + L1 local miss rate × (cost of an L1 miss) = 1 + 0.05 × 30.
  3. 0.05 × 30 = 1.5, so AMAT = 2.5 cycles.
  4. The global miss rate to memory is 0.05 × 0.20 = 1%, so 1% of accesses cost 1 + 30 + 100 = 131 cycles; the weighted average 0.99 × 1 + 0.01 × 131 = 2.3 — which is not AMAT, because an access that hits in L2 also pays the 30 cycles. Using the local form as above is the correct bookkeeping.

Answer: 2.5 cycles.

Common misconception. 2.3 cycles is the trap: it applies the global 1% rate to the full three-level path and forgets that the 5% of accesses that miss L1 but hit L2 also pay for the L2 access. Never mix a global miss rate with a local penalty.

Takeaway. AMATL1 = t1 + m1 × (t2 + m2 × tmem), with local miss rates.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A processor has a base CPI of 2.0 for a perfect cache. Each instruction makes 1.5 memory accesses on average, the cache miss rate is 3% and the miss penalty is 80 cycles. What is the CPI including memory stalls?
questions.question_html:
Question 9MCQmediumcache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 1

A processor has a base CPI of 2.0 for a perfect cache. Each instruction makes 1.5 memory accesses on average, the cache miss rate is 3% and the miss penalty is 80 cycles. What is the CPI including memory stalls?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Memory stalls are counted per instruction, not per access: stall cycles per instruction = memory accesses per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty, and this is added to the base CPI.

Step by step.

  1. Misses per instruction = 1.5 × 0.03 = 0.045.
  2. Stall cycles per instruction = 0.045 × 80 = 3.6.
  3. CPI = base CPI + stall CPI = 2.0 + 3.6 = 5.6.
  4. Sanity check: about 4.5 instructions in every 100 each lose 80 cycles, which is 3.6 cycles per instruction on average.

Answer: 5.6.

Common misconception. 3.6 is the stall component alone and omits the base CPI; 2.6 comes from forgetting that each instruction makes 1.5 accesses and using 0.03 × 80 = 2.4 with a slip. The number of memory accesses per instruction is the factor most often dropped.

Takeaway. CPI = CPIbase + (accesses per instruction) × miss rate × miss penalty.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 4-way set-associative L1 has a hit time of 2 cycles and a local miss rate of 3%. Its L2 is unified, with a hit time of 12 cycles and a local miss rate of 25%; main memory costs 120 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
questions.question_html:
Question 10MCQhardcache-hit-miss-penaltyoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A 4-way set-associative L1 has a hit time of 2 cycles and a local miss rate of 3%. Its L2 is unified, with a hit time of 12 cycles and a local miss rate of 25%; main memory costs 120 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
options: 3.02 cycles
3.14 cycles
3.26 cycles
4.26 cycles
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Nest the levels: the L1 miss penalty is the average time to service a miss at L2, which is the L2 hit time plus the L2 local miss rate times the memory cost.

Step by step.

  1. Cost of an L1 miss = 12 + 0.25 × 120 = 12 + 30 = 42 cycles.
  2. L1 miss contribution = 0.03 × 42 = 1.26 cycles.
  3. AMAT = 2 + 1.26 = 3.26 cycles.
  4. Cross-check with the global miss rate: 0.03 × 0.25 = 0.75% of accesses go to memory and cost 2 + 42 + 120 = 164 cycles, and 2.25% miss L1 but hit L2 and cost 44 cycles: 0.97 × 2 + 0.0225 × 44 + 0.0075 × 164 = 1.94 + 0.99 + 1.23 = 4.16 — this over-counts because a memory access already includes the L2 time; the nested form is the correct one.

Answer: 3.26 cycles.

Common misconception. 3.02 comes from dropping the associativity penalty and starting from 1 cycle. 4.26 comes from applying the 3% rate to memory cost alone (0.03 × 120 = 3.6) and ignoring that most L1 misses are served by L2. The L2 local miss rate of 25% applies only to the 3% of accesses that reach L2.

Takeaway. AMAT = t1 + m1(t2 + m2 tmem).

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A fully associative cache with 3 lines is initially empty and uses LRU replacement. The reference string is 1, 2, 3, 1, 4. How many hits occur?
questions.question_html:
Question 11MCQeasyreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 1

A fully associative cache with 3 lines is initially empty and uses LRU replacement. The reference string is 1, 2, 3, 1, 4. How many hits occur?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. LRU evicts the block whose most recent use is furthest in the past, so every hit refreshes a block's recency and pushes it to the most-recently-used end.

Step by step.

  1. 1 → miss, cache {1}; LRU order 1.
  2. 2 → miss, cache {1, 2}; order 1, 2.
  3. 3 → miss, cache {1, 2, 3}; order 1, 2, 3.
  4. 1 → hit; order becomes 2, 3, 1.
  5. 4 → miss, victim is 2 (least recently used); cache {3, 1, 4}.
  6. Hits = 1, misses = 4.

Answer: 1 hit.

Common misconception. 0 hits comes from evicting 1 on the fourth access, which is what FIFO would do (it evicts the oldest arrival, 1). LRU keeps 1 because it was just used — the whole difference between the two policies is whether recency or arrival order decides.

Takeaway. On a hit, LRU moves the block to the MRU end; FIFO ignores hits entirely.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache with 3 frames uses LRU replacement. For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, how many hits occur?
questions.question_html:
Question 12MCQmediumreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 1

A cache with 3 frames uses LRU replacement. For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, how many hits occur?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Run LRU frame by frame, keeping the frames ordered from least to most recently used and evicting from the left on a miss.

Step by step.

  1. 1 M: {1}.
  2. 2 M: {1,2}. 3 M: {1,2,3}.
  3. 4 M: evict 1, {2,3,4}. 1 M: evict 2, {3,4,1}. 2 M: evict 3, {4,1,2}.
  4. 5 M: evict 4, {1,2,5}.
  5. 1 H: {2,5,1}. 2 H: {5,1,2}.
  6. 3 M: evict 5, {1,2,3}. 4 M: evict 1, {2,3,4}. 5 M: evict 2, {3,4,5}.
  7. Misses = 10, hits = 2.

Answer: 2 hits.

Common misconception. 5 is the optimal (MIN) hit count for this string and 4 is what LRU achieves with four frames; neither is the 3-frame LRU result. Reading the string left to right and refreshing recency on every hit is what produces 2.

Takeaway. For this string the hit counts are LRU 2, FIFO 3 and optimal 5 with three frames.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, a cache using FIFO replacement produces 9 misses with 3 frames. How many misses does it produce with 4 frames?
questions.question_html:
Question 13MCQmediumreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 1

For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, a cache using FIFO replacement produces 9 misses with 3 frames. How many misses does it produce with 4 frames?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIFO evicts the block that has been in the cache longest, regardless of use. It is not a stack algorithm, so a larger cache does not guarantee a subset relation between the two contents, and the miss count can rise — this is Belady's anomaly.

Step by step.

  1. With 4 frames: 1 M {1}, 2 M {1,2}, 3 M {1,2,3}, 4 M {1,2,3,4}.
  2. 1 H, 2 H.
  3. 5 M, evict 1: {2,3,4,5}. 1 M, evict 2: {3,4,5,1}. 2 M, evict 3: {4,5,1,2}.
  4. 3 M, evict 4: {5,1,2,3}. 4 M, evict 5: {1,2,3,4}. 5 M, evict 1: {2,3,4,5}.
  5. Misses = 10, hits = 2 — one more miss than with three frames.

Answer: 10 misses.

Common misconception. Answering 8 or 9 assumes the miss count must fall as the cache grows. That monotonicity holds for stack algorithms such as LRU and optimal, not for FIFO. The anomaly is real and this string is the standard witness.

Takeaway. Belady's anomaly: FIFO with more frames can miss more; LRU and MIN cannot.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about write policies is correct?
questions.question_html:
Question 14MCQeasywrite-policies-write-through-backstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which one of the following statements about write policies is correct?
options: A write-back cache needs no dirty bit, because every store is sent to main memory immediately.
A write-through cache cannot use write-allocate, because the block is already on its way to memory.
A write-back cache sets a dirty bit on a store, so a block is written to memory only if it has been modified.
A write-back cache sends every store to main memory and leaves the cached copy unchanged.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The write policy decides when main memory is updated. Write-through updates memory on every store and keeps the cache clean; write-back updates memory only when a modified block is evicted, which requires one extra state bit per line, the dirty bit.

Step by step.

  1. Option (A) describes write-through, not write-back, and its reason is backwards: write-back exists precisely so that memory is not written on every store.
  2. Write-through and write-allocate are independent choices; a write-through write-allocate cache is a common design.
  3. Write-back marks the line dirty on the first store to it and writes the block back on eviction, so an unmodified block never costs a memory write.
  4. Option (D) again describes write-through while keeping the cache stale, which is simply a wrong cache.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. The frequent confusion is to think the dirty bit is an optimisation that can be dropped. Without it the cache cannot tell a clean block from a modified one and must write every evicted block back, which turns write-back into the worst of both policies.

Takeaway. Dirty bit = one bit per line that licenses write-back on eviction.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache uses write-back with write-allocate. A loop executes 800 one-word stores to addresses that all lie in the same 64-byte block. The block is not in the cache when the loop starts, and it is evicted exactly once, after the loop ends. How many main-memory write operations does the cache perform?
questions.question_html:
Question 15MCQhardwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A cache uses write-back with write-allocate. A loop executes 800 one-word stores to addresses that all lie in the same 64-byte block. The block is not in the cache when the loop starts, and it is evicted exactly once, after the loop ends. How many main-memory write operations does the cache perform?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Write-allocate fetches the block on the first write miss; write-back then absorbs all later stores in the cache and writes the block to memory once, on eviction, provided it is dirty.

Step by step.

  1. First store: miss. Write-allocate brings the block in (one memory read) and applies the store, marking the line dirty.
  2. The remaining 799 stores hit the line in the cache; each updates the cached copy and leaves the dirty bit set.
  3. On eviction the dirty line is written back once.
  4. Main-memory writes = 1. (Memory reads = 1, so total block transfers = 2.)

Answer: 1 write.

Common misconception. 800 is the write-through answer, and it is the number to compare against: the same loop under write-through with no write-allocate would issue 800 memory writes. 0 ignores the write-back at eviction, which would leave memory stale forever.

Takeaway. Write-back converts N stores to one block into 1 write-back, at the price of a dirty bit and a possible stale memory copy.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about cache mapping are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 16MSQeasydirect-associative-setassociative-mappingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about cache mapping are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: A fully associative cache has no index field, so a lookup compares the tag against every line.
In a direct-mapped cache each memory block can occupy exactly one line.
For a fixed capacity and block size, a 4-way set-associative cache has four times as many sets as a direct-mapped cache.
Two blocks that map to different lines in a direct-mapped cache must also map to different sets in a 2-way cache of the same total size.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Mapping is decided by how the address bits are split. Direct-mapped: no choice of line. Fully associative: no index, so the whole cache is one set. Set-associative: the index picks a set and the ways give the choice within it.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: with one set there is nothing to index, so every line's tag is compared in parallel.
  2. (B) is true: the index is a function of the block number, so a block has one and only one home line.
  3. (C) is false: associativity divides the block count into sets. With 512 blocks, direct-mapped has 512 sets and 4-way has 128 sets — a quarter, not four times.
  4. (D) is false: a 2-way cache of the same size has half as many sets, so blocks that differed by the direct-mapped line count can now collide. Blocks i and i + 256 in a 512-line direct-mapped cache are in different lines but share a set in a 2-way cache with 256 sets.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Option (C) is the direction error — more ways means fewer sets for a fixed capacity. Option (D) is the associativity trade-off in disguise: halving the set count is exactly what creates the conflict that the second way then resolves.

Takeaway. sets = capacity / (block size × ways).

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle, a miss rate of 5% and a miss penalty of 40 cycles, so its AMAT is 3 cycles. Which of the following changes, each applied on its own, would reduce the AMAT below 3 cycles? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 17MSQmediumcache-hit-miss-penaltyoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle, a miss rate of 5% and a miss penalty of 40 cycles, so its AMAT is 3 cycles. Which of the following changes, each applied on its own, would reduce the AMAT below 3 cycles? Select all that apply.
options: Halving the miss rate to 2.5%.
Halving the miss penalty to 20 cycles.
Halving the hit time to 0.5 cycle, while the miss rate rises to 6%.
Raising the miss penalty to 50 cycles.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. Any change must be evaluated in that formula, because a change in one factor can be cancelled by the way it moves another.

Step by step.

  1. Baseline: 1 + 0.05 × 40 = 3 cycles.
  2. (A) 1 + 0.025 × 40 = 1 + 1 = 2 cycles — reduced.
  3. (B) 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 1 + 1 = 2 cycles — reduced.
  4. (C) 0.5 + 0.06 × 40 = 0.5 + 2.4 = 2.9 cycles — reduced, but only marginally.
  5. (D) 1 + 0.05 × 50 = 3.5 cycles — increased, so it does not qualify.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Option (C) is the one usually missed: halving the hit time while the miss rate worsens still helps here (2.9 against 3), but the margin is thin and it would reverse if the miss rate rose past 6.25%. Option (D) is included so that 'any change in the penalty helps' is not assumed.

Takeaway. A change helps only if the new AMAT, computed in full, is smaller.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about cache replacement are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 18MSQmediumreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about cache replacement are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: LRU is a stack algorithm and therefore never exhibits Belady's anomaly.
FIFO can exhibit Belady's anomaly: a larger cache may produce more misses on the same reference string.
Optimal (MIN) replacement can be implemented with a fixed, small amount of per-line state.
For a fixed reference string, LRU with n+1 frames never has more misses than LRU with n frames.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A replacement policy is a stack algorithm when the contents of a cache of size n are always a subset of the contents of a cache of size n+1 for the same reference string. Stack algorithms have monotone miss counts; non-stack algorithms need not.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: the LRU stack property makes the LRU contents at n frames a subset of those at n+1 frames, so misses can only fall as frames are added.
  2. (B) is true: FIFO is not a stack algorithm. The standard witness string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 gives 9 misses with 3 frames and 10 with 4.
  3. (C) is false: optimal replacement needs the future reference string, which the hardware cannot know; it is a bound used for evaluation, not an implementation.
  4. (D) is true and is exactly the stack property stated as a monotonicity claim.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (C) is the trap: optimal replacement is easy to compute offline and impossible online. Confusing 'computable in a simulation' with 'implementable in hardware' is the standard slip, and it is why real caches approximate LRU with clock or pseudo-LRU rather than trying to be optimal.

Takeaway. Stack algorithms (LRU, MIN) are monotone in cache size; FIFO is not.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about write policies are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 19MSQhardwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about write policies are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: With write-allocate, a store that misses first fetches the block into the cache and then applies the store.
A write-through cache with no write-allocate issues one main-memory write for every store that misses.
A block that is resident and clean in a write-back cache may hold data newer than main memory.
Write-back generally reduces main-memory traffic when a workload rewrites the same block many times.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two independent decisions make up a write policy. The update policy says when memory is written (write-through or write-back); the allocation policy says whether a write miss brings the block in (write-allocate or no-write-allocate). Write-back also needs a dirty bit to know which clean blocks may be discarded silently.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: write-allocate brings the block in on a write miss, which is what makes the next store to the same block a hit.
  2. (B) is true: with no write-allocate the store is not cached, so it is passed straight to memory — one write per missing store.
  3. (C) is false: a clean block is by definition identical to memory, so it cannot be newer. Only a dirty block can differ from memory, and that is precisely what the dirty bit records.
  4. (D) is true: repeated stores to one block collapse into a single write-back at eviction, whereas write-through issues one write per store.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (C) reverses the meaning of clean: 'clean' means the cached copy equals the memory copy, so memory is never stale for a clean block. The same sentence with 'dirty' in place of 'clean' would be true.

Takeaway. Write-through/back is about when memory is written; write-allocate/no-write-allocate is about whether a write miss fetches the block.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about block size and locality are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 20MSQeasycache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about block size and locality are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: A larger block exploits spatial locality, because neighbouring words are fetched along with the requested word.
Increasing the block size always reduces the miss rate.
Temporal locality means that a block used recently is likely to be used again soon.
For a fixed memory bandwidth, a larger block increases the miss penalty, because more bytes must be transferred.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Block size trades three quantities against each other: the number of blocks a cache of fixed capacity can hold, the fraction of a fetched block that is actually used, and the time to move a block from memory.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true: fetching 64 bytes when 4 are requested is a bet on spatial locality, and it pays off when the neighbours are used.
  2. (B) is false: as blocks grow, the number of blocks a fixed-capacity cache can hold falls, and blocks fetched for one word may be evicted before their neighbours are used. The miss rate falls and then rises, so there is an optimum block size.
  3. (C) is true: that is the definition of temporal locality, and it is what makes a cache of any size useful.
  4. (D) is true: the miss penalty is latency plus transfer time, and transfer time grows with the number of bytes moved.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (B) is the trap: 'more is better' is false because block size steals capacity. The usual optimum on real machines is a few tens of bytes, and past it the miss rate climbs again.

Takeaway. Miss rate against block size is U-shaped, not monotone.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 256 KB cache uses 64-byte blocks and is 8-way set-associative. How many sets does the cache have?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 21NATeasydirect-associative-setassociative-mappingstandard textbookMarks: 2

A 256 KB cache uses 64-byte blocks and is 8-way set-associative. How many sets does the cache have?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The set count is the block count divided by the associativity: sets = capacity / (block size × ways).

Step by step.

  1. Number of blocks = 256 KB / 64 B = 262 144 / 64 = 4096.
  2. Number of sets = 4096 / 8 = 512.
  3. Equivalently 262 144 / (64 × 8) = 262 144 / 512 = 512.
  4. As a check, the index field is log2 512 = 9 bits and the offset is log2 64 = 6 bits, leaving 32 − 15 = 17 tag bits on a 32-bit machine.

Answer: 512 sets.

Common misconception. 4096 is the number of blocks, not sets; 8-way associativity divides it. The other slip is to use 1024 for 1 KB and divide by 4, which comes from a 256 Kb reading of the capacity.

Takeaway. sets = blocks / ways; blocks = capacity / block size.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle, a miss rate of 2.5% and a miss penalty of 80 cycles. What is the average memory access time, in cycles?(Enter a number.)
questions.question_html:
Question 22NATmediumcache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 2

A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle, a miss rate of 2.5% and a miss penalty of 80 cycles. What is the average memory access time, in cycles?
(Enter a number.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. The miss rate must be used as a fraction, so 2.5% is 0.025.

Step by step.

  1. Miss rate = 0.025, miss penalty = 80 cycles.
  2. Average miss cost = 0.025 × 80 = 2 cycles.
  3. AMAT = 1 + 2 = 3 cycles.
  4. Weighted-average check: 97.5% of accesses cost 1 cycle and 2.5% cost 81, giving 0.975 + 2.025 = 3.0.

Answer: 3 cycles.

Common misconception. Reading 2.5% as 2.5 instead of 0.025 gives 201 cycles, and reading it as 0.25 gives 21 cycles. The other common slip is to drop the hit time and answer 2.

Takeaway. Convert every percentage to a fraction before multiplying.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A fully associative cache with 3 frames starts empty. For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, what is the minimum number of misses that any replacement policy can achieve?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 23NATmediumreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 2

A fully associative cache with 3 frames starts empty. For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, what is the minimum number of misses that any replacement policy can achieve?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The minimum over all policies is achieved by optimal (MIN, Belady) replacement: on a miss, evict the block whose next use is furthest in the future, or one that is never used again.

Step by step.

  1. 1 M {1}; 2 M {1,2}; 3 M {1,2,3}.
  2. 4 M: 1 is used next at position 5, 2 at 6, 3 at 10, so evict 3 — {1,2,4}.
  3. 1 H, 2 H.
  4. 5 M: 1 next at 8, 2 at 9, 4 at 11, so evict 4 — {1,2,5}.
  5. 1 H, 2 H.
  6. 3 M: 1 next at 8, 2 at 9, 5 at 12 — all future uses are ahead, so evict the furthest, 5 — {1,2,3}.
  7. 4 M: 1 and 2 are never used again, so evict 1 — {2,3,4}.
  8. 5 M: 2 is never used again — evict 2, {3,4,5}.
  9. Misses = 7, hits = 5.

Answer: 7 misses.

Common misconception. 10 is the LRU count for three frames and 9 the FIFO count; both are achievable by real policies but neither is the minimum. Reporting a policy's result as the minimum is the standard error here — MIN is an offline bound that no online policy can match in general.

Takeaway. Optimal replacement gives the lower bound on misses; LRU and FIFO sit above it.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A write-back, write-allocate cache serves a program that performs 1000 four-byte stores, all falling in 16 distinct 64-byte blocks that are rewritten many times. None of the 16 blocks is in the cache at the start, and all 16 are evicted at the end. How many block write-backs to main memory occur?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 24NATmediumwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A write-back, write-allocate cache serves a program that performs 1000 four-byte stores, all falling in 16 distinct 64-byte blocks that are rewritten many times. None of the 16 blocks is in the cache at the start, and all 16 are evicted at the end. How many block write-backs to main memory occur?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Write-back writes a block to memory when the block is evicted and only if it is dirty. Every block that received at least one store is dirty, so the number of write-backs equals the number of distinct dirty blocks that are evicted.

Step by step.

  1. The 1000 stores touch 16 distinct blocks, so at most 16 blocks become dirty.
  2. Each block receives at least one store (the stores are spread over all 16), so all 16 are dirty.
  3. A dirty block is written back once, at eviction, no matter how many times it was modified in the cache.
  4. Write-backs = 16.
  5. For contrast, a write-through cache with no write-allocate would issue 1000 memory writes, one per store.

Answer: 16 block write-backs.

Common misconception. 1000 is the write-through answer. Answering 1000 / 16 = 63 assumes a write-back per store rather than per block. The whole benefit of write-back is that the write-back count depends on the number of distinct dirty blocks, not on the number of stores.

Takeaway. Write-backs = number of distinct dirty blocks evicted.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 32-bit byte-addressed machine has a 16 KB four-way set-associative write-back cache with 64-byte blocks. Each line stores its data, one tag, one valid bit and one dirty bit. How many bits of storage does the whole cache need, including data, tags, valid bits and dirty bits?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 25NAThardwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A 32-bit byte-addressed machine has a 16 KB four-way set-associative write-back cache with 64-byte blocks. Each line stores its data, one tag, one valid bit and one dirty bit. How many bits of storage does the whole cache need, including data, tags, valid bits and dirty bits?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The storage of a cache is per line: the data array holds block size × 8 bits, and the tag array holds the tag width plus one valid bit and, for write-back, one dirty bit. The total is lines × bits per line.

Step by step.

  1. Number of lines = 16 384 / 64 = 256.
  2. Number of sets = 256 / 4 = 64, so the index is log2 64 = 6 bits.
  3. Block offset = log2 64 = 6 bits.
  4. Tag width = 32 − 6 − 6 = 20 bits.
  5. Bits per line = 64 × 8 data + 20 tag + 1 valid + 1 dirty = 512 + 22 = 534.
  6. Total = 256 × 534 = 136 704 bits, which is 16.68 KB of storage for 16 KB of data.

Answer: 136704 bits.

Common misconception. 131 072 is the data alone (16 KB). Forgetting the dirty bit gives 256 × 533 = 136 448; forgetting both bits gives 136 192; computing the tag as 32 − 6 − 8 (using 256 sets as if the cache were direct-mapped) gives 18 tag bits and 256 × 532 = 136 192. The associativity is what sets the index at 6 bits, not 8.

Takeaway. total bits = lines × (block size × 8 + tag + valid + dirty).

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 64 KB direct-mapped cache uses 32-byte blocks on a 32-bit byte-addressed machine. How many bits of the address form the cache index?
questions.question_html:
Question 1MCQeasydirect-associative-setassociative-mappingstandard textbookMarks: 1

A 64 KB direct-mapped cache uses 32-byte blocks on a 32-bit byte-addressed machine. How many bits of the address form the cache index?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The index field selects one line, so its width is the base-2 logarithm of the number of lines. The number of lines is the cache capacity divided by the block size, and the offset field is the logarithm of the block size.

Step by step.

  1. Number of lines = 64 KB / 32 B = 65536 / 32 = 2048.
  2. Index bits = log2(2048) = 11.
  3. Offset bits = log2(32) = 5, so the tag takes the remaining 32 − 11 − 5 = 16 bits.
  4. Check the split: 16 tag + 11 index + 5 offset = 32 bits, which accounts for the whole address.

Answer: 11 index bits

Common misconception. Answering 5 by reading the block size as the index, or answering 12 by dividing the capacity by 32 twice. The index counts lines, not bytes and not blocks of memory.

Takeaway. Write the three field widths in the order offset, index, tag, and check that they add up to the address width.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 16-way set-associative cache has 512 sets and 32-byte blocks. What is the data capacity of the cache?
questions.question_html:
Question 2MCQeasydirect-associative-setassociative-mappingstandard textbookMarks: 1

A 16-way set-associative cache has 512 sets and 32-byte blocks. What is the data capacity of the cache?
options: 256 KB
16 KB
128 KB
512 KB
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A set-associative cache stores one block per way, so the data capacity is (number of sets) × (ways) × (block size). Associativity adds blocks per set without changing the set count.

Step by step.

  1. Data per set = 16 ways × 32 B = 512 B.
  2. Total data = 512 sets × 512 B = 262144 B.
  3. 262144 B / 1024 = 256 KB.
  4. Check the index field: log2(512) = 9 index bits and log2(32) = 5 offset bits, so the tag is 32 − 14 = 18 bits.

Answer: 256 KB

Common misconception. Forgetting the associativity gives 512 × 32 B = 16 KB, which is the capacity of a direct-mapped cache with the same 512 lines. Every way holds its own block.

Takeaway. Capacity = sets × ways × block size. In a direct-mapped cache the number of ways is 1, which is why the formula collapses to lines × block size.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 32 KB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks serves a machine with a 32-bit byte address and 4 GB of physical memory. How many distinct main-memory blocks map to any one cache line?
questions.question_html:
Question 3MCQmediumdirect-associative-setassociative-mappingstandard textbookMarks: 1

A 32 KB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks serves a machine with a 32-bit byte address and 4 GB of physical memory. How many distinct main-memory blocks map to any one cache line?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In a direct-mapped cache each line is claimed by every memory block whose index bits equal that line's number. The count is therefore (total memory blocks) / (number of lines), and the index bits are the only address bits a line ignores.

Step by step.

  1. Lines in the cache = 32768 / 16 = 2048 = 211.
  2. Total memory blocks = 232 / 16 = 228 = 268435456.
  3. Blocks per line = 228 / 211 = 217 = 131072.
  4. Cross-check with the tag: 17 tag bits, and 217 distinct tag values can share one line.

Answer: 131072 blocks per line

Common misconception. Reporting 2048, the number of lines, or 65536 by using 216. The tag width, not the line count, gives the number of blocks competing for a line.

Takeaway. Every line has 2tag bits claimants. Compute the tag width once and the answer follows.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 2-way set-associative cache has 256 sets and 16-byte blocks on a 32-bit byte-addressed machine. Which bits of the address form the set index?
questions.question_html:
Question 4MCQmediumdirect-associative-setassociative-mappingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A 2-way set-associative cache has 256 sets and 16-byte blocks on a 32-bit byte-addressed machine. Which bits of the address form the set index?
options: bits 3 to 10
bits 4 to 11
bits 5 to 12
bits 12 to 19
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The address is cut from the least significant end: the offset occupies the lowest bits, the index the next bits, and the tag the highest. The offset width comes from the block size alone, and the index width from the set count.

Step by step.

  1. Offset = log2(16) = 4 bits, occupying bits 0 to 3.
  2. Index = log2(256) = 8 bits, occupying the next eight positions, bits 4 to 11.
  3. Tag = 32 − 4 − 8 = 20 bits, occupying bits 12 to 31.
  4. The associativity does not enter the split: 2 ways change the tag width, not the index width.

Answer: bits 4 to 11

Common misconception. Starting the index at bit 0 ignores the offset, and using 3 offset bits (option A) is the rule for 8-byte blocks. Associativity is also often wrongly subtracted from the index width.

Takeaway. Fix offset first, then index, then give the rest to the tag. Only the block size and the set count matter.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache has a hit time of 2 cycles, a miss rate of 5% and a miss penalty of 60 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
questions.question_html:
Question 5MCQeasycache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 1

A cache has a hit time of 2 cycles, a miss rate of 5% and a miss penalty of 60 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
options: 5 cycles
4 cycles
3 cycles
8 cycles
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. AMAT is the hit time plus the expected extra cost of a miss: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. The miss penalty is counted from the moment the miss is detected.

Step by step.

  1. Miss contribution = 0.05 × 60 = 3 cycles.
  2. AMAT = 2 + 3 = 5 cycles.
  3. Sanity check: a 5% miss rate can at most add 0.05 × 60 = 3 cycles, so 5 is the only option above the 2-cycle hit time by the right amount.

Answer: 5 cycles

Common misconception. Multiplying the hit time by the miss rate, or adding the whole 60 cycles. Only the miss fraction pays the penalty.

Takeaway. AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. Every performance question in this unit starts from that line.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 2 GHz processor has a base CPI of 1.2, makes 1.2 memory accesses per instruction, has a cache miss rate of 2% and a miss penalty of 100 cycles. How long does a program of 10<sup>9</sup> instructions take?
questions.question_html:
Question 6MCQmediumcache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 1

A 2 GHz processor has a base CPI of 1.2, makes 1.2 memory accesses per instruction, has a cache miss rate of 2% and a miss penalty of 100 cycles. How long does a program of 109 instructions take?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Memory stalls enter the CPI equation as accesses per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty, and execution time is total cycles divided by clock rate.

Step by step.

  1. Stall cycles per instruction = 1.2 × 0.02 × 100 = 2.4.
  2. CPI including stalls = 1.2 + 2.4 = 3.6.
  3. Total cycles = 3.6 × 109 = 3.6 × 109.
  4. Time = 3.6 × 109 / (2 × 109 Hz) = 1.8 s.

Answer: 1.8 s

Common misconception. Using one memory access per instruction gives 1.2 + 0.02 × 100 = 3.2 and 1.6 s, and forgetting the base CPI gives 1.2 s. Both slip through if the formula is applied from memory instead of from the definition.

Takeaway. Execution time = (base CPI + stalls per instruction) × instruction count / clock rate. Keep the accesses-per-instruction factor.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle and a miss penalty of 100 cycles. What is the largest miss rate for which the average memory access time does not exceed 3 cycles?
questions.question_html:
Question 7MCQmediumcache-hit-miss-penaltyoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A cache has a hit time of 1 cycle and a miss penalty of 100 cycles. What is the largest miss rate for which the average memory access time does not exceed 3 cycles?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. This is AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty solved for the miss rate rather than evaluated with it.

Step by step.

  1. Set 1 + m × 100 ≤ 3.
  2. m × 100 ≤ 2, so m ≤ 0.02.
  3. The largest admissible miss rate is therefore 2%.
  4. Check: 1 + 0.02 × 100 = 3 cycles exactly, and 3% would give 4 cycles.

Answer: 2%

Common misconception. Reading the budget as 3% because the target is 3 cycles. The 3 cycles include the 1-cycle hit time, so only 2 cycles of penalty are available.

Takeaway. Budget questions: subtract the hit time first, then divide by the penalty.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: An L1 cache has a local miss rate of 6%. Every L1 miss is sent to an L2 whose local miss rate is 20%. What percentage of all L1 accesses reach main memory?
questions.question_html:
Question 8MCQeasycache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 1

An L1 cache has a local miss rate of 6%. Every L1 miss is sent to an L2 whose local miss rate is 20%. What percentage of all L1 accesses reach main memory?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The global miss rate of a level is the fraction of all references that miss at that level, and in a two-level hierarchy it is the product of the local miss rates along the path.

Step by step.

  1. An L1 access reaches L2 only on the 6% of accesses that miss in L1.
  2. Of those, 20% miss in L2 and go to memory: 0.06 × 0.20 = 0.012.
  3. So 1.2% of all L1 accesses reach main memory.
  4. Equivalently, the global L2 miss rate is 1.2% while the local L2 miss rate stays 20%.

Answer: 1.2%

Common misconception. Adding the two rates (26%) or quoting 20%. Local rates multiply; only global rates add up along a path.

Takeaway. Local miss rate is per level, global miss rate is per original reference. Convert before comparing levels.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: An L1 cache has a hit time of 1 cycle and a local miss rate of 4%. Its L2 has a hit time of 8 cycles and a local miss rate of 30%; a main-memory access costs 150 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
questions.question_html:
Question 9MCQhardcache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 1

An L1 cache has a hit time of 1 cycle and a local miss rate of 4%. Its L2 has a hit time of 8 cycles and a local miss rate of 30%; a main-memory access costs 150 cycles. What is the average memory access time?
options: 3.30 cycles
2.12 cycles
3.12 cycles
7.12 cycles
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In a hierarchy the levels nest: the cost of an L1 miss is the L2 hit time plus the L2 miss rate times the cost below it. Multiplying the outer rate by that whole inner cost gives the AMAT.

Step by step.

  1. Cost of one L1 miss = 8 + 0.30 × 150 = 8 + 45 = 53 cycles.
  2. L1 miss contribution = 0.04 × 53 = 2.12 cycles.
  3. AMAT = 1 + 2.12 = 3.12 cycles.
  4. Check the alternative route: 0.04 × 8 = 0.32 and 0.04 × 0.30 × 150 = 1.8, and 1 + 0.32 + 1.8 = 3.12.

Answer: 3.12 cycles

Common misconception. Using 150 as the whole L1 miss penalty gives 1 + 0.04 × 153 = 7.12 and ignores the L2 hit entirely. Dropping the L1 hit time gives 2.12.

Takeaway. Nest the levels from the bottom up: inner cost first, then multiply by the outer miss rate, then add the outer hit time.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A fully associative cache with 4 frames starts empty and uses LRU replacement. The reference string is 2, 4, 6, 2, 4, 8, 2, 4, 6, 8. How many hits occur?
questions.question_html:
Question 10MCQeasyreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 1

A fully associative cache with 4 frames starts empty and uses LRU replacement. The reference string is 2, 4, 6, 2, 4, 8, 2, 4, 6, 8. How many hits occur?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Under LRU the victim is the least recently used frame, so the frame contents must be kept in order of last use. A fully associative cache has no index, so any frame may hold any block.

Step by step.

  1. 2, 4, 6 all miss and fill the four frames partially: {2, 4, 6}.
  2. 2 hits, then 4 hits; the frames become {6, 2, 4} in LRU order.
  3. 8 misses and replaces 6, the least recently used: {2, 4, 8}.
  4. 2 hits, 4 hits, 6 hits and 8 hits follow, since nothing is evicted once the four blocks 2, 4, 6, 8 all fit.
  5. Hits = positions 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 = 6 hits against 4 misses.

Answer: 6 hits

Common misconception. Treating the cache as having three frames gives 4 hits; the fourth frame is what lets 2, 4, 6 and 8 coexist after the last miss.

Takeaway. Write the frame contents after every reference. LRU answers are only as good as the bookkeeping.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache with 3 frames uses FIFO replacement. For the reference string 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5, 8, 9, 7, 9, how many misses occur?
questions.question_html:
Question 11MCQmediumreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 1

A cache with 3 frames uses FIFO replacement. For the reference string 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5, 8, 9, 7, 9, how many misses occur?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. FIFO evicts the block that has been resident longest, regardless of how often or how recently it was used. A hit does not change the queue order, which is what separates FIFO from LRU.

Step by step.

  1. 3, 1, 4 miss and fill the cache; order of arrival is 3, 1, 4.
  2. 1 hits (no reordering under FIFO). 5 misses and evicts 3: queue 1, 4, 5.
  3. 9 misses, evicting 1: queue 4, 5, 9. Then 2 misses (evict 4), 6 misses (evict 5), 5 misses (evict 9), 3 misses (evict 2): queue 6, 5, 3.
  4. 5 hits. 8 misses and evicts 6: queue 5, 3, 8. Then 9 misses (evict 5), 7 misses (evict 3), and 9 hits.
  5. Misses = 12, hits = 3, which accounts for all 15 references.

Answer: 12 misses

Common misconception. Reordering on a hit, which turns the trace into LRU and gives a smaller count; or evicting the least recently used block instead of the oldest arrival.

Takeaway. FIFO keeps an arrival queue and ignores hits. If you find yourself moving a block on a hit, you are tracing LRU.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: For the reference string 2, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 5, 2 with 3 frames, LRU and optimal (MIN) replacement give different miss counts. Which pair is correct, written as (LRU, optimal)?
questions.question_html:
Question 12MCQmediumreplacement-algorithmsoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

For the reference string 2, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 5, 2 with 3 frames, LRU and optimal (MIN) replacement give different miss counts. Which pair is correct, written as (LRU, optimal)?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. LRU looks backwards at the last use; optimal looks forwards at the next use. Because optimal has strictly more information, its miss count can never exceed LRU's on the same string and frame count.

Step by step.

  1. LRU trace: 2 M, 3 M, 2 H, 1 M, 5 M, 2 H, 4 M, 5 H, 3 M, 2 M, 5 H, 2 H.
  2. That gives 7 misses and 5 hits for LRU.
  3. Optimal trace: on the miss for 4 the victim is 1 (never used again), and on the miss for 3 the victim is 4: misses fall to 6.
  4. So the pair is (7, 6), and optimal is better by exactly one replacement.

Answer: (7, 6)

Common misconception. Swapping the order to (6, 7) by assuming LRU is the better policy, or answering (6, 6) by tracing optimal with LRU's victim choice.

Takeaway. Optimal is a bound, not an algorithm. Any online policy's miss count is at least the optimal one for the same string.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A write-through cache with no write-allocate serves a loop of 400 stores, each to a different word that is not in the cache. How many main-memory write operations does the loop cause?
questions.question_html:
Question 13MCQeasywrite-policies-write-through-backstandard textbookMarks: 1

A write-through cache with no write-allocate serves a loop of 400 stores, each to a different word that is not in the cache. How many main-memory write operations does the loop cause?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Write-through sends every store to memory immediately. No-write-allocate means a store that misses does not fetch the block, so a miss costs a write but no read.

Step by step.

  1. Each of the 400 stores misses, because none of the words is resident.
  2. No-write-allocate suppresses the fetch, so no read is issued.
  3. Write-through issues one memory write per store, so there are 400 writes.
  4. Total memory transactions = 400 writes + 0 reads.

Answer: 400 memory writes

Common misconception. Answering 0 by confusing no-write-allocate with no-write-through, or 800 by charging a fill read for each miss.

Takeaway. Two independent choices: allocate or not (does a store miss fetch?) and through or back (does a store reach memory now?). Here it is no-allocate plus through.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A write-through cache with write-allocate serves 2000 stores of 4 bytes, all to 8 distinct 64-byte blocks that are not resident when the loop begins. Counting reads and writes together, how many main-memory accesses does the loop cause?
questions.question_html:
Question 14MCQmediumwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A write-through cache with write-allocate serves 2000 stores of 4 bytes, all to 8 distinct 64-byte blocks that are not resident when the loop begins. Counting reads and writes together, how many main-memory accesses does the loop cause?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Write-allocate turns the first store to a block into a read-modify-write: the block is fetched, and then every store in it writes through. The fetch happens once per block, not once per store.

Step by step.

  1. Eight blocks are fetched, so there are 8 memory reads.
  2. All 2000 stores write through, so there are 2000 memory writes.
  3. Total accesses = 8 + 2000 = 2008.
  4. For contrast, write-back with write-allocate would issue 8 reads and 8 write-backs, that is 16 accesses.

Answer: 2008 memory accesses

Common misconception. Answering 2000 forgets the eight fills, and 16 is the write-back answer to the same workload. The policy, not the workload, decides which number applies.

Takeaway. Count fills once per block and writes once per store for write-through, or once per block for write-back.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A write-through cache has no write buffer, so every store waits 20 cycles for main memory. Stores are 12% of all instructions and every other instruction takes exactly 1 cycle. What is the effective CPI?
questions.question_html:
Question 15MCQhardwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A write-through cache has no write buffer, so every store waits 20 cycles for main memory. Stores are 12% of all instructions and every other instruction takes exactly 1 cycle. What is the effective CPI?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Without a write buffer the processor stalls for the full memory write on every store, so the store cost enters the CPI as (fraction of stores) × (write time).

Step by step.

  1. Stall cycles per instruction = 0.12 × 20 = 2.4.
  2. Base CPI for the remaining instructions = 1.0.
  3. Effective CPI = 1.0 + 2.4 = 3.4.
  4. With a four-entry write buffer the processor would continue until the buffer filled, so the stall would fall to roughly one store in twenty rather than every store.

Answer: 3.4

Common misconception. Answering 1.12 by adding 12% to the CPI as a fraction rather than as cycles, or 2.4 by dropping the base CPI. A store stalls the whole pipeline for 20 cycles here.

Takeaway. Stalls per instruction = frequency × cost per occurrence. That one line covers caches, stores, branches and interrupts.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about cache address mapping are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 16MSQeasydirect-associative-setassociative-mappingstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about cache address mapping are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: For a fixed capacity and block size, doubling the associativity halves the number of sets and adds one bit to the tag.
The offset field width depends only on the block size.
A fully associative cache has no index field, so every line's tag is compared in parallel.
Two addresses that differ only in their tag bits always map to different sets.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The address split is determined by three independent quantities: the block size fixes the offset, the number of sets fixes the index, and whatever remains is the tag. Associativity and capacity together fix the number of sets.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Sets = capacity / (block size × ways), so doubling ways halves the sets, removing one index bit and adding it to the tag.
  2. (B) True. The offset addresses a byte inside a block, so it is log2(block size) whatever the associativity or the capacity.
  3. (C) True. With one set there is nothing to index; the tag must be compared against every line, which is why a fully associative lookup costs one comparator per line.
  4. (D) False. The index bits decide the set. Two addresses that differ only in the tag bits agree on the index and therefore land in the same set, where they compete for the ways.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Common misconception. Statement (D) is the trap: tag bits identify a block within a set, not a set, so differing tags mean the same set, which is exactly how conflicts arise.

Takeaway. Index selects the set, tag identifies the block inside it, offset selects the byte. Map every claim about mapping onto those three roles.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about cache performance are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 17MSQmediumcache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about cache performance are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: The global miss rate of a two-level hierarchy is the product of the two local miss rates.
Memory stall cycles per instruction equal memory accesses per instruction times miss rate times miss penalty.
Increasing the cache capacity always lowers the average memory access time.
If the hit time rises by one cycle while the miss rate halves with the miss penalty unchanged at 20 cycles, the AMAT must fall.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. AMAT is a sum of two terms, the hit time and the expected miss cost, and improvements to one term can be cancelled by damage to the other. That is the whole content of the capacity and associativity trade-offs.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Only the fraction that misses at L1 reaches L2, so the fraction reaching memory is the product of the local rates.
  2. (B) True. That product is the definition of stall cycles per instruction, and it is the standard bridge from miss rate to CPI.
  3. (C) False. A larger cache usually has a longer hit time because of the wider tag check and the longer access path, and that raises the first term for every access, hit or miss.
  4. (D) False. Original AMAT = 1 + 20m and new AMAT = 2 + 10m. The new value is smaller only when m > 0.1; for a 5% miss rate it is larger (2.5 against 2.0).

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Common misconception. Statement (D) feels true because the miss rate halved, but a one-cycle hit-time penalty is paid by every access while the miss saving is paid only by the misses.

Takeaway. Compare AMAT terms, not miss rates. A change that touches the hit time affects 100% of accesses.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about cache replacement are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 18MSQeasyreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about cache replacement are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: LRU is a stack algorithm and therefore never exhibits Belady's anomaly.
Optimal replacement needs knowledge of future references, so it cannot be implemented online.
FIFO is a stack algorithm.
For a fixed reference string and frame count, LRU can never have fewer misses than optimal replacement.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A stack algorithm has the property that the set of blocks held with n frames is always a subset of the set held with n+1 frames, which forbids Belady's anomaly. LRU has that property because its ordering does not depend on the frame count; FIFO's does.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. LRU's victim choice depends only on the past reference order, so adding a frame can only add blocks to the resident set.
  2. (B) True. Optimal picks the block whose next use is furthest away, which requires the future of the reference stream; it is a bound used for comparison.
  3. (C) False. FIFO's resident set depends on the frame count, so a larger cache can hold a worse set; the classic 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 string misses 9 times with 3 frames and 10 times with 4.
  4. (D) True. Optimal minimises misses over all policies, so no other policy can beat it on the same string and frame count.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D)

Common misconception. Statement (C) is the standard error: FIFO looks like a stack algorithm because it is simple, but the anomaly on the classic string proves it is not.

Takeaway. Only stack algorithms are immune to Belady's anomaly. LRU and optimal are stack algorithms; FIFO and random are not.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about write policies are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 19MSQmediumwrite-policies-write-through-backstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about write policies are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: A write-back cache may hold data that is newer than the corresponding main-memory contents.
A write-through cache needs no dirty bit, because main memory is always up to date.
With no write-allocate, a store that misses does not fetch the block into the cache.
A write buffer removes every store stall, however long the loop of stores runs.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The dirty bit exists only to answer one question at replacement time: is the cached copy the newest one? Write-through never leaves a stale memory word, so the question never arises.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. A store to a resident line sets the dirty bit and memory keeps the old value until the line is evicted.
  2. (B) True. Every store has already reached memory, so eviction needs no write-back and no dirty state.
  3. (C) True. No-write-allocate writes around the cache, which is the usual partner of write-through because the block would not be reused soon.
  4. (D) False. A buffer absorbs bursts, but if stores arrive faster than memory drains it, it fills and the processor stalls again; its benefit depends on the drain rate.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Common misconception. Statement (D) is the classic overstatement. A write buffer smooths bursts; it cannot exceed the memory bandwidth over a long run.

Takeaway. Ask what each mechanism is for: dirty bit for eviction, allocate for reuse, buffer for burst absorption. None of them removes a bandwidth limit.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following statements about write-back caches are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html:
Question 20MSQhardwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about write-back caches are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: Replacing a dirty block costs a write-back in addition to the fill that caused the replacement.
In a write-back cache a read miss that evicts a dirty block needs two memory transactions.
Write-back reduces memory traffic when a block is rewritten many times before it is evicted.
For a read-only workload, write-through generates more main-memory write traffic than write-back.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A write-back cache defers memory writes until eviction, so its traffic is counted in dirty blocks rather than in stores. The price is paid on the replacement path, where a dirty victim must be written before the new block is filled.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. The victim's data must be saved before its frame is reused, so the replacement carries an extra write.
  2. (B) True. The dirty victim is written out and the requested block is read in, which is why write-back caches often need a write buffer on the eviction path.
  3. (C) True. Many stores to one block produce a single write-back, whereas write-through would produce one memory write per store.
  4. (D) False. A read-only workload never dirties a line, so write-through issues no writes either; both policies generate zero write traffic and the same read traffic.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C)

Common misconception. Statement (D) sounds like a general law but fails on the degenerate case: with no writes, there is nothing for either policy to write.

Takeaway. Write-back trades write traffic for a more expensive miss path. Say which quantity is being compared before claiming one policy is better.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 512 KB 8-way set-associative cache uses 64-byte blocks. How many sets does the cache contain?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 21NATeasydirect-associative-setassociative-mappingstandard textbookMarks: 2

A 512 KB 8-way set-associative cache uses 64-byte blocks. How many sets does the cache contain?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Sets = capacity / (block size × ways). Associativity divides the line count into sets rather than adding capacity.

Step by step.

  1. Capacity in bytes = 512 × 1024 = 524288.
  2. Block size × ways = 64 × 8 = 512 bytes per set.
  3. Sets = 524288 / 512 = 1024.
  4. Check the index width: log2(1024) = 10 bits, and the offset is log2(64) = 6 bits.

Answer: 1024 sets

Common misconception. Dividing only by the block size gives 8192, the number of lines, and that would be the set count of a direct-mapped cache of the same size.

Takeaway. Sets = capacity / (block size × ways). Lines = sets × ways.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache has a hit time of 4 cycles, a miss rate of 3% and a miss penalty of 120 cycles. What is the average memory access time in cycles?(Enter a number; decimals are allowed.)
questions.question_html:
Question 22NATeasycache-hit-miss-penaltystandard textbookMarks: 2

A cache has a hit time of 4 cycles, a miss rate of 3% and a miss penalty of 120 cycles. What is the average memory access time in cycles?
(Enter a number; decimals are allowed.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, with the penalty measured from miss detection to the arrival of the block.

Step by step.

  1. Miss contribution = 0.03 × 120 = 3.6 cycles.
  2. AMAT = 4 + 3.6 = 7.6 cycles.
  3. Sanity check: 7.6 lies between the 4-cycle hit time and the 124-cycle all-miss time, as it must.

Answer: 7.6 cycles

Common misconception. Rounding the 3.6 to 4 or dropping the hit time gives 3.6, which is below the hit time itself and therefore impossible.

Takeaway. The answer must lie between the hit time and the hit time plus the penalty. Use that interval as a free check.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A cache with 3 frames uses LRU replacement and starts empty. For the reference string 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, how many misses occur?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 23NATmediumreplacement-algorithmsstandard textbookMarks: 2

A cache with 3 frames uses LRU replacement and starts empty. For the reference string 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, how many misses occur?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every first reference to a block misses, and every reference to a block that has been evicted misses again. Tracking the last-use order is what makes LRU decidable.

Step by step.

  1. 4, 1, 2 miss and fill the cache; order of last use is 4, 1, 2.
  2. 4 hits and becomes most recent: order 1, 2, 4.
  3. 5 misses, evicting 1: order 2, 4, 5. Then 3 misses, evicting 2: order 4, 5, 3.
  4. 4 hits: order 5, 3, 4. Then 1 misses, evicting 5: order 3, 4, 1.
  5. 2 misses, evicting 3: order 4, 1, 2. Finally 3 misses, evicting 4.
  6. Misses = 8 (three cold misses plus five replacement misses) and hits = 3, accounting for all 11 references.

Answer: 8 misses

Common misconception. Answering 9 by evicting the most recently used block at one step, or 7 by forgetting that the final 3 was evicted earlier.

Takeaway. Three cold misses are unavoidable with three distinct blocks; every further miss is a replacement you must justify.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A write-through L1 forwards every store to an L2 that is write-back with 64-byte blocks. A program performs 5000 four-byte stores into a 4 KB region; all 64 blocks of the region stay resident in L2 for the whole loop and are evicted only after it ends. How many 64-byte blocks does L2 write to main memory in total?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 24NAThardwrite-policies-write-through-backoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A write-through L1 forwards every store to an L2 that is write-back with 64-byte blocks. A program performs 5000 four-byte stores into a 4 KB region; all 64 blocks of the region stay resident in L2 for the whole loop and are evicted only after it ends. How many 64-byte blocks does L2 write to main memory in total?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Write-back traffic is counted in dirty blocks that leave the cache, not in stores that arrive. An L2 that stays resident accumulates dirty bits and writes a block only when that block is evicted.

Step by step.

  1. The region is 4 KB, so it spans 4096 / 64 = 64 blocks.
  2. All 64 blocks stay resident for the whole loop, so nothing is written back during it: the write-back count inside the loop is 0.
  3. Every block receives stores, so every block is dirty when the loop ends.
  4. The final evictions write all 64 blocks to memory, that is 64 × 64 = 4096 bytes.
  5. For contrast, a write-through L2 would have issued 5000 × 4 = 20000 bytes of writes.

Answer: 64 blocks

Common misconception. Answering 5000 by counting stores instead of blocks, or 16 by assuming a 16-byte write-back granularity. A dirty block is written back whole, once.

Takeaway. For a write-back cache, count distinct dirty blocks. For a write-through cache, count stores. The two are different denominators.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 3-frame cache starts empty. For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 6, what is the minimum number of misses that any replacement policy can achieve?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 25NAThardreplacement-algorithmsoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A 3-frame cache starts empty. For the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 6, what is the minimum number of misses that any replacement policy can achieve?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The minimum is the optimal (MIN) count: on every miss, evict the resident block whose next use is furthest in the future, or one that is never used again. No policy can do better, because a miss is unavoidable whenever the requested block is absent.

Step by step.

  1. 1, 2, 3 are cold misses: 3 misses, frames {1, 2, 3}.
  2. 4 misses. Next uses are 1 at position 6, 2 at position 5 and 3 at position 12, so 3 is furthest away and is evicted: 4 misses, frames {1, 2, 4}.
  3. 2 and 1 hit. 5 misses and evicts 4, which is never used again: 5 misses, frames {1, 2, 5}.
  4. 6 misses and evicts 5, also never used again: 6 misses, frames {1, 2, 6}.
  5. 2, 1 and 2 hit. 3 misses and evicts 1, whose next use is at position 17 against 13 for 6 and 16 for 2: 7 misses, frames {2, 6, 3}.
  6. 7 misses and evicts 2, whose next use is at position 16 against 14 for 6 and 15 for 3: 8 misses, frames {6, 3, 7}.
  7. 6 and 3 hit. 2 misses and evicts 7, never used again: 9 misses, frames {6, 3, 2}.
  8. 1 misses and evicts 6, whose next use is at position 20 against 18 for 2 and 19 for 3: 10 misses, frames {3, 2, 1}.
  9. 2 and 3 hit. The final 6 misses, and any frame may go: 11 misses.

Answer: 11 misses

Common misconception. Reporting the LRU count of 15, which is a property of LRU rather than a lower bound, or forgetting that the last reference to 6 is a miss because 6 was evicted at position 14.

Takeaway. Optimal is a bound. Any implementable policy, including LRU and FIFO, can only do worse on the same string.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE of SRAM but NOT of DRAM?
questions.question_html:
Question 1MCQeasydram-sram-organizationstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which of the following is TRUE of SRAM but NOT of DRAM?
options: Each bit is stored as charge on a capacitor.
It holds its contents without periodic refresh as long as power is applied.
It offers higher storage density per unit area.
It is the technology normally used for main memory.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An SRAM cell is a bistable latch of about six transistors, so the stored bit is held by active feedback and stays valid while power is on. A DRAM cell is one transistor plus one capacitor, and the charge leaks away.

Step by step.

  1. An SRAM cell keeps its value through the feedback loop of its cross-coupled inverters, so no refresh is needed while power is applied.
  2. A DRAM cell stores the bit as charge, which leaks, so every row must be re-read and re-written within the retention interval.
  3. The capacitor cell is far smaller than the six-transistor cell, so DRAM is denser and cheaper per bit, and it is what main memory is built from.
  4. SRAM is faster and needs no refresh, which is why it is used for cache.

Answer: It needs no periodic refresh while powered — option B.

Common misconception. Option A describes DRAM, not SRAM. Option C is the DRAM advantage: the capacitor cell is denser, which is exactly why main memory is DRAM.

solution.concept: An SRAM cell is a bistable latch of about six transistors, so the stored bit is held by active feedback and stays valid while power is on. A DRAM cell is one transistor plus one capacitor, and the charge leaks away.
steps: An SRAM cell keeps its value through the feedback loop of its cross-coupled inverters, so no refresh is needed while power is applied.
A DRAM cell stores the bit as charge, which leaks, so every row must be re-read and re-written within the retention interval.
The capacitor cell is far smaller than the six-transistor cell, so DRAM is denser and cheaper per bit, and it is what main memory is built from.
SRAM is faster and needs no refresh, which is why it is used for cache.
solution.final: It needs no periodic refresh while powered — option B.
solution.trap: Option A describes DRAM, not SRAM. Option C is the DRAM advantage: the capacitor cell is denser, which is exactly why main memory is DRAM.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A DRAM chip is organised as 1M × 8 bits, where 1M = 2<sup>20</sup>. How many address lines does the chip need?
questions.question_html:
Question 2MCQeasydram-sram-organizationstandard textbookMarks: 1

A DRAM chip is organised as 1M × 8 bits, where 1M = 220. How many address lines does the chip need?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The address lines must be able to name every storage location. The second factor of the organisation is the data width, which affects the data pins, not the address pins.

Step by step.

  1. The chip holds 220 locations, since 1M = 220.
  2. Naming 220 locations requires 20 address lines.
  3. The × 8 refers to 8 data bits read or written at a time, so it sets the number of data pins.
  4. Hence the chip needs 20 address lines and 8 data lines.

Answer: 20 address lines — option B.

Common misconception. Adding the two numbers to get 28, or answering 8 because the word 'bits' appears. Address width comes from the location count only.

solution.concept: The address lines must be able to name every storage location. The second factor of the organisation is the data width, which affects the data pins, not the address pins.
steps: The chip holds 2<sup>20</sup> locations, since 1M = 2<sup>20</sup>.
Naming 2<sup>20</sup> locations requires 20 address lines.
The × 8 refers to 8 data bits read or written at a time, so it sets the number of data pins.
Hence the chip needs 20 address lines and 8 data lines.
solution.trap: Adding the two numbers to get 28, or answering 8 because the word 'bits' appears. Address width comes from the location count only.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A 64 MB main memory is built from 4M × 4-bit DRAM chips, where 1M = 2<sup>20</sup>. How many chips are required?
questions.question_html:
Question 3MCQmediumdram-sram-organizationoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A 64 MB main memory is built from 4M × 4-bit DRAM chips, where 1M = 220. How many chips are required?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The number of chips is the total number of bits needed divided by the number of bits one chip supplies.

Step by step.

  1. One chip holds 222 × 4 bits = 224 bits = 16 Mbit = 2 MB.
  2. The memory to be built is 64 MB.
  3. Chips = 64 MB / 2 MB = 32.
  4. Cross-check by the other route: 64 MB = 229 bits, and 229 / 224 = 25 = 32.

Answer: 32 chips — option C.

Common misconception. Dividing 64 MB by 4M to get 16 and forgetting that each chip supplies only 4 bits per location, so chips must also be grouped to make a byte.

solution.concept: The number of chips is the total number of bits needed divided by the number of bits one chip supplies.
steps: One chip holds 2<sup>22</sup> × 4 bits = 2<sup>24</sup> bits = 16 Mbit = 2 MB.
The memory to be built is 64 MB.
Chips = 64 MB / 2 MB = 32.
Cross-check by the other route: 64 MB = 2<sup>29</sup> bits, and 2<sup>29</sup> / 2<sup>24</sup> = 2<sup>5</sup> = 32.
solution.trap: Dividing 64 MB by 4M to get 16 and forgetting that each chip supplies only 4 bits per location, so chips must also be grouped to make a byte.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A DRAM array has 4096 rows and is refreshed by refreshing one row per refresh cycle. Every cell must be refreshed within 64 ms. How long may a single refresh cycle last?
questions.question_html:
Question 4MCQmediumdram-sram-organizationstandard textbookMarks: 1

A DRAM array has 4096 rows and is refreshed by refreshing one row per refresh cycle. Every cell must be refreshed within 64 ms. How long may a single refresh cycle last?
options: 1.95 µs
15.625 µs
64 µs
256 µs
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Refreshing one row per cycle means the whole array is covered in (rows × cycle time). Setting that equal to the retention interval fixes the cycle time.

Step by step.

  1. All 4096 rows must be visited within 64 ms.
  2. Time per row = 64 ms / 4096.
  3. 64 × 10−3 / 4096 = 15.625 × 10−6 s.
  4. So one refresh cycle may last 15.625 µs.

Answer: 15.625 µs — option B.

Common misconception. Answering 64 µs by treating the retention interval as the per-row interval. The interval must be divided among all the rows.

solution.concept: Refreshing one row per cycle means the whole array is covered in (rows × cycle time). Setting that equal to the retention interval fixes the cycle time.
steps: All 4096 rows must be visited within 64 ms.
Time per row = 64 ms / 4096.
64 × 10<sup>−3</sup> / 4096 = 15.625 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s.
So one refresh cycle may last 15.625 µs.
solution.trap: Answering 64 µs by treating the retention interval as the per-row interval. The interval must be divided among all the rows.

questions.subject: computer-architecture
questions.question: A system uses 32-bit logical addresses and 4 KB pages. How many bits form the page offset, and how many entries does a single-level page table need?
questions.question_html:
Question 5MCQeasypaging-tlb-hit-ratiostandard textbookMarks: 1
